clue.text: School gives one the boot

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a well-known English public school
second meaning: a rubber knee-high boot, named after the Duke

explanation.surface: A school expels a pupil, giving them the boot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gives one the boot' reads as expulsion, but 'the boot' is simply a kind of boot; a wellington is a rubber rain boot, called a gumboot elsewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Wellington College is a famous English boarding school, and a wellington is a waterproof rubber boot reaching the knee.

clue.text: Diffidence, to Giant Despair

parts.note: surface reading: a quality of shyness or lack of confidence
setter's reading: in Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, Diffidence is the name of the spouse of Giant Despair of Doubting Castle

explanation.walkthrough: Diffidence looks like an abstract noun, but in The Pilgrim's Progress it is a character's name, the giant's spouse.
explanation.definitionFit: In Bunyan's allegory Giant Despair is married to a woman named Diffidence, who counsels him on torturing the pilgrims.

clue.text: Adornment to which Johnson likened Greek

definitions.text: Adornment to which Johnson likened Greek

parts.note: surface reading: some decoration or ornament
setter's reading: Samuel Johnson said Greek is like this delicate fabric, since every man gets as much of it as he can

explanation.walkthrough: Boswell records Johnson saying that Greek, like this openwork trimming, is something every man acquires as much of as he can.
explanation.definitionFit: Lace is an openwork decorative fabric used to trim clothing, so it is an adornment, and Johnson's quoted simile names it.

clue.text: Bury in blame maybe, for going on and on

parts.note: to inter is to bury a body

indicators.note: 'maybe' says the preceding letters are only one possible arrangement, so they may be rearranged

parts.note: letters taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone buried in reproach, endlessly going on about it.
explanation.walkthrough: INTER plus a rearrangement of IN BLAME (MINABLE) gives INTERMINABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Interminable describes something seemingly endless, tediously lasting so long it never seems to stop.

clue.text: Evidence of action to beat receiving

definitions.text: Evidence of action to beat receiving

parts.note: surface reading: proof that something was done
setter's reading: the saying that it is more blessed to give than to receive, so these are proof of the better act

explanation.walkthrough: The clue alludes to Acts 20:35, 'It is more blessed to give than to receive'; presents are the evidence of giving.
explanation.definitionFit: Presents handed over are tangible proof that someone has done the giving, the act said to surpass receiving.

clue.text: They all informed against Hamlet

parts.note: surface reading: a group of informers betraying someone
setter's reading: a soliloquy in Act 4 where the prince says that every chance event seems to reproach him for his delay

explanation.walkthrough: The clue quotes Hamlet, Act 4 Scene 4, where events seem to reproach the prince for his delay.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's line the events and circumstances around Hamlet are what rebuke him, and the play calls them occasions.

clue.text: Foil getting into the peepshow

indicators.note: something getting into a phrase sits inside its words, so look within the letters

parts.note: run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A sword or a sheet of foil sneaks into a peepshow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foil' suggests kitchen foil or thwarting, but it is the fencing weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are fencing swords, so one weapon stands for another of the same sport as a near synonym.

clue.text: Favourable so support it with promissory notes

parts.note: a prop is a support
taken as written
an IOU is a written promise to pay

explanation.surface: Good terms offered: back it with written promises to pay.
explanation.definitionFit: Propitious conditions are auspicious, likely to bring success, so the adjective means favourable.

clue.text: Arranged to dine with Green

indicators.note: to arrange things is to put them in a new order, so the letters are set out afresh

parts.note: taken as written
as printed the clue is one letter short; the setter probably wrote Greene, the novelist

explanation.surface: A dinner date fixed up with someone called Green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arranged' does double duty as definition and anagram signal. As printed the fodder lacks one E, so the source probably read Greene.
explanation.definitionFit: To engineer something is to contrive or organise it skilfully, so engineered means arranged or brought about.

clue.text: No such confrontation of miners when on strike

definitions.text: No such confrontation of miners when on strike

parts.note: surface reading: an industrial dispute where no meeting takes place
setter's reading: miners work at the coal face, and on strike none of them is at the face

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase for meeting in person is read literally: striking miners are never facing the coal face.
explanation.definitionFit: Face to face means in direct personal confrontation, two parties meeting eye to eye.

clue.text: Caller for dinner going without one

indicators.note: 'without' means lacking, so the following item is taken out

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone summoning guests to dinner goes off without anyone.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove I from GOING to leave GONG.
explanation.definitionFit: A dinner gong is struck in grand houses to summon the household to the table, so it calls people to eat.

clue.text: Behaved like a star or with

definitions.text: Behaved like a star or with

parts.note: surface reading: acting like a celebrity; setter's reading: twinkled, as a star in the sky does
setter's reading: the clue seems cut short, probably 'or with wit', the word's other sense of being brilliantly clever

explanation.walkthrough: 'Star' tempts you towards a celebrity, but the sense is a twinkling heavenly body. The printed clue appears truncated after 'with'.
explanation.definitionFit: To scintillate is to sparkle or twinkle, and figuratively to be dazzlingly lively or witty in conversation.

clue.text: Sample of people in Banbury?

parts.note: surface reading: a representative group drawn from a population
setter's reading: Banbury is known for its Cross, from the nursery rhyme 'Ride a cock-horse to Banbury Cross', so a part of it

explanation.walkthrough: Banbury is an English market town famous for its Cross in the nursery rhyme; a section of that cross is a playful sample.
explanation.definitionFit: A cross-section is a representative sample of a population, showing all its typical kinds of members.

clue.text: Definition of Cinderella's aim at billiards?

parts.note: setter's reading: the fairy-tale heroine's goal was the royal dance, so her aim was getting to that event
surface reading: a cue-sports term for the ball a player tries to hit with the cue ball

explanation.walkthrough: Cinderella's objective was the prince's ball; in billiards the phrase names the ball the cue ball must strike.
explanation.definitionFit: In billiards and snooker the object ball is the target struck by the cue ball, as opposed to the cue ball itself.

clue.text: Help to break the cane — that's a relief

parts.note: to assist is to help

indicators.note: to break something is to smash it into bits that can be put back in another order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is glad of a hand to snap a cane, or of escape from a caning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Help' looks like the definition, but it is wordplay; the definition is relief in its charitable sense, at the far end.
explanation.definitionFit: Relief in the sense of aid given to those in need, such as famine relief, is assistance.

clue.text: Mikado-style punishment for foot faults?

parts.note: surface reading: a penalty in the comic Japan of Gilbert and Sullivan, and the word ends with the same -ado
setter's reading: not a tennis serving error but a beating on the soles of the feet

explanation.walkthrough: A foot fault is a tennis serving offence; here the punishment is literally delivered to the feet. The Mikado is a Gilbert and Sullivan opera about fitting punishments.
explanation.definitionFit: The bastinado is a torture or punishment of beating the soles of the feet with a stick.

clue.text: Shares producing yield for a digger

definitions.meaning: first meaning: portions distributed, as when stock is allotted to applicants
second meaning: a rented plot where a gardener grows vegetables

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shares' and 'yield' suggest finance, but the second sense is a garden plot; in Britain an allotment is a small rented patch for growing vegetables.
explanation.definitionFit: An allotment is both a portion allocated to someone and a small piece of rented land cultivated for produce.

clue.text: "After battle sleep is best, after — tranquillity" (Noel)

definitions.text: "After battle sleep is best, after — tranquillity" (Noel)

parts.words: "After battle sleep is best, after — tranquillity"
parts.note: surface reading: a line of verse with one word missing
setter's reading: the line is by the poet Roden Noel, and the gap is filled by the opposite of tranquillity

explanation.walkthrough: Fill the blank in Roden Noel's line; the missing word must contrast with tranquillity as battle contrasts with sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: Din and clamour are the opposite of calm, and the poet pairs this loud sound with the quiet that should follow.

clue.text: Farrar's boy has a girl

parts.note: Dean Farrar wrote the Victorian school story 'Eric, or Little by Little'
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man named Farrar has a son and a daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: Erica is a feminine given name, so it serves as a girl in the usual crossword sense of a name.

clue.text: With us details can produce weariness

indicators.note: to produce something is to make it from raw material, so the letters are worked into new form

parts.note: letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Being made to handle all the details wears a team out.
explanation.definitionFit: Lassitude is a state of physical or mental tiredness and lack of energy, so it means weariness.

clue.text: Not a jot of the idle talk in this gossip?

parts.note: a tittle is a tiny amount, as in 'not one jot or tittle'
to tattle is to chatter idly

explanation.surface: Asks whether this gossip holds any trace of real chatter.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface echoes the biblical 'not one jot or tittle'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tittle-tattle is idle chatter about other people's affairs, the same thing as gossip.

clue.text: Work in the driver's place for capital cover

indicators.note: 'in' places the first item inside the next

parts.note: a golfer drives from the tee
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Taking over the chauffeur's seat to fetch a hat in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The driver is a golfer, not a motorist. 'Capital' means head, not a city.
explanation.definitionFit: A topee is a lightweight sun helmet worn in the tropics, and it covers the head, here called the capital.

clue.text: Time for shooting her?

parts.note: surface reading: the hour when executions by firing squad traditionally take place
setter's reading: the answer is also a woman's name, so 'her' points to a girl

explanation.walkthrough: Firing squads and wildfowlers go out at first light, and the same word is a girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Daybreak is the traditional hour for executions and duck shooting, and it is also a feminine given name.

clue.text: She's among the best in service at the bar

definitions.note: a pronoun standing for a woman

indicators.note: 'among' says to look inside the words that follow

parts.note: runs across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A bartender who ranks among the best in the trade.
explanation.walkthrough: Hebe was cupbearer to the Greek gods, and her name was old slang for a barmaid.
explanation.definitionFit: Hebe, the goddess who served nectar to the gods, gave her name to a waitress or barmaid serving drinks.

clue.text: Charley had one from Brazil

parts.note: surface reading: a man owning something
setter's reading: the title relative in Brandon Thomas's Victorian farce comes 'from Brazil, where the nuts come from'

explanation.walkthrough: Brandon Thomas's farce Charley's Aunt turns on an impostor posing as the rich relative from Brazil.
explanation.definitionFit: In the play the title character is Charley's father's sister, a wealthy widow from South America.

clue.text: Peter, eat up — one way to keep going

indicators.note: 'one way' suggests one possible ordering among many, so the letters may be set out differently

parts.note: letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A parent urges Peter to finish his meal to keep his strength up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eat up' sounds like the instruction, but 'up' belongs to the letters too.
explanation.definitionFit: To perpetuate something is to make it continue indefinitely, to preserve and prolong it.

clue.text: Thus willingly to exist is faith

parts.note: setter's reading: an old word for gladly, as in 'I would as soon'
surface reading: a maxim that living means believing, with the four-letter word for existence lurking in a near-identical spelling

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is loose: the answer is spelt almost like the word for existence, hinted by 'to exist'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lief is an archaic adverb meaning gladly or readily, surviving in the phrase 'I'd as lief'.

clue.text: Those present given time for a fling

parts.note: 'at ten' is a time of day
a Highland fling is a dance

explanation.surface: Guests are told what hour to arrive for a party.
explanation.definitionFit: Attendance is the number of people who are there at an event, the gathering of those present.
